title: MIRROR: Learning from the Other View for Multi-Modal Reasoning
authors: Wen Ye, Yuxiao Qu, Aviral Kumar, Xuezhe Ma
abstract: Unlike large language models (LLMs) that exhibit strong reasoning capabilities, vision-language models (VLMs) struggle with visual reasoning, even on geometry problems that admit equivalent text, diagram, and combined diagram+text views. We show that these views often elicit different behaviors: a model may solve a problem from text but fail on the corresponding diagram, or succeed visually while failing textually. This inconsistency suggests that different views expose complementary reasoning paths and failure modes that standard multimodal post-training does not fully exploit. To study and exploit this phenomenon, we construct ODA-Data, a high-quality paired multimodal geometry dataset with text-dominant, image-dominant, and combined image+text views of the same problems, together with splits for training and evaluating modality-dependent reasoning behaviors. We then develop Modality-Informed Reciprocal Reasoning Optimization (MIRROR), a reinforcement learning approach for improving multimodal reasoning via self supervision. For each problem, MIRROR evaluates the model under all views, selects the best-performing view as a teacher, and trains other views with a reverse-KL objective towards the teacher. Across reasoning benchmarks that evaluate on geometry problems, MIRROR improves over standard RL and yields more accurate and consistent behavior across modalities

infographic.key_insight: MIRROR exploits the fact that text, image, and combined views of the same geometry problem reveal complementary reasoning strengths and failures, using the best view to teach the others.
infographic.engineering_relevance: This provides a practical training recipe for making vision-language models more reliable and consistent across modalities in multimodal reasoning systems.
method: Build ODA-Data: paired geometry problems with text-dominant, image-dominant, and combined views.
Evaluate the model on all views for each problem and choose the best-performing view as the teacher.
Apply a reverse-KL reinforcement learning objective to align weaker views toward the teacher view.
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract reports improvements over standard RL across geometry reasoning benchmarks, with better accuracy and more consistent behavior across modalities.
infographic.watch_item: The approach depends on high-quality paired multimodal data and view-wise evaluation, so gains may be sensitive to dataset construction and teacher-view selection.
infographic.paper_title: MIRROR: Learning from the Other View for Multi-Modal Reasoning

title: PATS: Policy-Aware Training Scaffolding for Agentic Reinforcement Learning
authors: Yipeng Shi, Zhipeng Ma, Yue Wang, Qitai Tan, Yang Li, Peng Chen
abstract: In long-horizon LLM agent reinforcement learning, weak policies often repeat similar failures, producing uninformative rollout trajectories and limiting effective policy optimization. Existing skill-centric methods improve exploration by optimizing, filtering, or internalizing reusable skills. However, they remain centered on the skills themselves rather than being designed as adaptive training-time support for the evolving policy. To address this, we propose a policy-centric training paradigm that reframes skills as a dynamic training scaffold. Our framework, Pats, converts rollout groups from the latest policy into evidence cards and uses task-specific evaluation to adjust the context used in subsequent rollouts. Concrete guidance helps weak policies to complete challenging tasks. As policy improves, redundant context is revised or removed to reduce reliance on explicit guidance while preserving useful rollout variation. The policy is optimized with environmental rewards using standard RLVR, and the training scaffold is discarded at deployment. On ALFWorld and WebShop, Pats improves over strong baselines by up to 18.6%. Across seven search-augmented QA benchmarks, it remains competitive while using 32.1% fewer prompt tokens than the baseline.

infographic.key_insight: PATS turns training-time skills into a policy-aware scaffold that adapts guidance as the agent improves, instead of treating skills as fixed reusable artifacts.
infographic.engineering_relevance: It offers a practical RLVR training strategy for long-horizon LLM agents that can improve task success while reducing prompt-token cost during training.
method: Convert rollout groups from the latest policy into evidence cards.
Use task-specific evaluation to revise, add, or remove context for later rollouts.
Train with environmental rewards under standard RLVR; discard the scaffold at deployment.
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract reports gains of up to 18.6% on ALFWorld and WebShop, and competitive results on seven search-augmented QA benchmarks with 32.1% fewer prompt tokens than the baseline.
infographic.watch_item: Because the scaffold is dynamically adjusted from recent rollouts, performance may depend on reliable task-specific evaluation and careful control of when guidance is removed.
infographic.paper_title: PATS: Policy-Aware Training Scaffolding for Agentic Reinforcement Learning

title: Graph Neural Network Force Fields (GPTFF-mol) for Organic Molecules from Optimization Trajectories (OpenGEM26)
authors: Yifan Huang, Fankai Xie, Jiangnan Zheng, Tenglong Lu, Sheng Meng, Miao Liu
abstract: Density functional theory (DFT) serves as a reliable tool for atomistic molecular simulations, while machine learning potentials have become powerful complements to balance accuracy and efficiency. In this work, we release OpenGEM26 (Open Generated Ensemble of Molecules, 2026), a large-scale dataset comprising 200,000 unique molecules and 4.4 million conformations composed of H, C, N, O, S and Cl with up to ten heavy atoms. All calculations are carried out at the ωB97X-D/Def2-SVP and Def2-TZVP levels with dispersion corrections, and complete structural optimization trajectories and abundant non-equilibrium structures are recorded. Statistical analyses confirm that this dataset covers a broader conformational space than QM9 in terms of energy, bond lengths and bond angles. A graph neural network-based potential GPTFF-mol is trained using the new dataset, achieving an energy mean absolute error of 16 meV/molecule, which is equivalent to 0.82meV/atom, and superior force prediction performance compared with ANI-2x. Validated by butane rotation and keto-enol tautomerization tests, the model accurately describes molecular dynamical behaviors and reaction barriers at distorted geometries. This work provides a high-quality resource and robust ML potential for efficient simulations of sulfur- and chlorine-containing organic molecules.

infographic.key_insight: OpenGEM26 expands molecular machine-learning force-field training with 4.4 million DFT conformations from 200,000 organic molecules, enabling GPTFF-mol to model energies and forces more accurately across broader chemical and conformational space.
infographic.engineering_relevance: This provides a practical surrogate for DFT in atomistic simulation of sulfur- and chlorine-containing organics, reducing computational cost while preserving reliable geometry, dynamics, and barrier predictions.
method: Built OpenGEM26 from optimization trajectories and non-equilibrium structures for H/C/N/O/S/Cl molecules with up to ten heavy atoms.
Computed labels at ωB97X-D/Def2-SVP and Def2-TZVP with dispersion corrections.
Trained a graph neural network potential, GPTFF-mol, on the resulting large-scale dataset.
infographic.evidence_signal: The paper reports GPTFF-mol reaches 16 meV/molecule (0.82 meV/atom) energy MAE and outperforms ANI-2x on force prediction, while reproducing butane rotation and keto-enol tautomerization behavior.
infographic.watch_item: Performance is demonstrated on molecules with up to ten heavy atoms, so generalization to larger chemistries or very different reaction classes may require additional validation.
infographic.paper_title: Graph Neural Network Force Fields (GPTFF-mol) for Organic Molecules from Optimization Trajectories (OpenGEM26)

title: AREX: Towards a Recursively Self-Improving Agent for Deep Research
authors: Shuqi Lu, Chaofan Li, Kun Luo, Zhang Zhang, Hui Wang, Hongwang Xiao
abstract: Deep research requires agents to find answers that jointly satisfy multiple constraints. Discovering such answers is costly, whereas verifying a candidate can often be decomposed into tractable constraint-wise checks. This discovery--verification asymmetry suggests that a research agent should do more than simply search longer: it should recursively improve its current answer by verifying intermediate results and using the partially verified state to guide subsequent refinement. We introduce AREX, a family of Recursively Self-Improving (RSI) deep research agents. AREX alternates between an inner research loop that gathers evidence and constructs a provisional answer, and an outer self-improvement loop that audits the answer constraint-wise, identifies unresolved claims, and launches targeted follow-up research. To sustain RSI over long horizons, AREX learns an autonomous context-update tool that compresses growing interaction history into a compact improvement state preserving verified evidence and unresolved constraints, without relying on an external model. We train AREX on verified synthetic tasks and high-quality trajectories through agentic mid-training and long-horizon reinforcement learning. To mitigate sparse final rewards during long horizon learning, we emphasize key steps where decisive evidence is acquired or erroneous research directions are corrected. We instantiate a dense 4B model and a 122B-A10B Mixture-of-Experts model. Across BrowseComp, WideSearch, DeepSearchQA, Humanity's Last Exam (HLE), and other reasoning and tool-use benchmarks, AREX substantially outperforms comparable-scale baselines and remains competitive with models using substantially more activated parameters.

infographic.key_insight: AREX improves deep-research agents by recursively refining answers through constraint-wise verification, using verified partial results to drive targeted follow-up research.
infographic.engineering_relevance: This suggests a practical agent design pattern for long-horizon research systems: separate answer discovery from verification, and compress history into a compact state to sustain iterative self-improvement.
method: Inner loop gathers evidence and drafts a provisional answer.
Outer loop audits the answer constraint by constraint, flags unresolved claims, and triggers focused follow-up research.
An autonomous context-update tool compresses the interaction history into a compact improvement state without an external model.
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract reports training on verified synthetic tasks and high-quality trajectories, then evaluating across BrowseComp, WideSearch, DeepSearchQA, Humanity's Last Exam (HLE), and other reasoning/tool-use benchmarks, where AREX outperforms comparable-scale baselines.
infographic.watch_item: Recursive self-improvement depends on reliable verification and context compression; errors in the audit step or information loss in the improvement state could compound over long horizons.
infographic.paper_title: AREX: Towards a Recursively Self-Improving Agent for Deep Research

title: Compact Latent Coordination for Autonomous Vehicles at Unsignalized Intersections
authors: Gil Lifshits, Igal Bilik, Gilad Katz
abstract: Coordinating autonomous vehicles at unsignalized intersections remains a critical challenge for multi-agent reinforcement learning (MARL) systems, which typically struggle with combinatorial action spaces, reliance on privileged information, or rigid agent designs. We propose Master-Agent Proto-plan System (MAPS), a hierarchical deep reinforcement learning (DRL) architecture in which a centralized Master agent generates a compact, continuous embedding, denoted as proto-plan, that encodes a global coordination strategy. Decentralized Worker agents integrate this embedding with local observations to execute vehicle-specific control, decoupling strategic intent from tactical execution and enabling independent optimization of each module. As a proof-of-concept evaluation of this coordination mechanism, we test MAPS across 72 intersection configurations in HighwayEnv. MAPS achieves collision-free navigation while significantly reducing average travel time, outperforming state-of-the-art baselines. The learned proto-plans further exhibit robust generalization: a system trained with three agents achieves a 94% success rate when deployed zero-shot to five-agent scenarios, confirming that proto-plan-based hierarchical learning provides a promising framework for multi-vehicle coordination.

infographic.key_insight: MAPS uses a centralized continuous "proto-plan" to coordinate decentralized vehicle control, separating global strategy from local execution for better multi-agent intersection handling.
infographic.engineering_relevance: This architecture offers a practical way to scale autonomous vehicle coordination at unsignalized intersections while improving safety, travel time, and zero-shot generalization across agent counts.
method: Master agent produces a compact latent proto-plan for global coordination.
Worker agents combine the proto-plan with local observations for vehicle-level control.
Hierarchical design supports independent optimization of strategy and tactics.
infographic.evidence_signal: Evaluated in HighwayEnv across 72 intersection configurations, MAPS achieved collision-free navigation, reduced average travel time, and reached a 94% success rate when trained with three agents and deployed zero-shot to five agents.
infographic.watch_item: Results are shown in simulation, so real-world performance may depend on sensing noise, traffic uncertainty, and transfer to physical vehicles.
infographic.paper_title: Compact Latent Coordination for Autonomous Vehicles at Unsignalized Intersections

title: An LLM-Driven Workflow for Automated Process Control Strategy Generation and Tuning from Dynamic Process Models
authors: Ari Luna Rueda, Eike Cramer, Klaus Hellgardt, Mehmet Mercangöz
abstract: We present a structured large-language-model-driven workflow for automated multi-variable control design from dynamic process models. The workflow decomposes the design task into constrained code-generation steps: plant-interface construction, normalization, manipulated-variable controlled-variable (MV-CV) pairing, controller specification, closed loop simulation, scenario generation, performance evaluation and Bayesian-optimization (BO) based tuning. Generated artifacts are executed and validated before downstream tasks proceed, and failed artifacts are repaired using validation feedback. The proposed approach is demonstrated on a nonlinear gas-preheater benchmark with coupled pressure and temperature dynamics. The generated workflow produces a physically consistent decentralized PI (proportional-integral) feedback-feedforward control structure and an executable tuning environment. Bayesian optimization reduces the closed loop performance objective, which aggregates set-point tracking and disturbance-rejection errors for the controlled variables, by approximately 26.5% relative to the initial controller generated by the workflow, mainly through improved pressure-loop transient performance. This figure quantifies the automated tuning stage rather than a comparison against a manually designed controller. The results demonstrate the feasibility of using structured large-language-model-based code generation to construct executable control-design workflows, while also highlighting the need for broader validation on larger plantwide-control benchmarks.

infographic.key_insight: A structured LLM workflow can automatically generate, validate, and tune an executable multivariable control strategy directly from a dynamic process model.
infographic.engineering_relevance: This offers a practical path to faster control-design prototyping for nonlinear plants, with automated code generation and Bayesian tuning of decentralized PI/PF controllers.
method: Decompose control design into constrained LLM code-generation steps: plant interface, normalization, MV-CV pairing, controller specification, simulation, scenario generation, and evaluation.
Execute and validate each generated artifact before proceeding; repair failed steps using validation feedback.
Use Bayesian optimization to tune controller parameters against a closed-loop objective combining tracking and disturbance-rejection errors.
infographic.evidence_signal: On a nonlinear gas-preheater benchmark, the workflow produced a physically consistent decentralized PI feedback-feedforward controller, and Bayesian optimization reduced the closed-loop objective by about 26.5% versus the initially generated controller.
infographic.watch_item: The result is demonstrated on a single benchmark, so broader validation is still needed to confirm robustness on larger plantwide-control problems.
infographic.paper_title: An LLM-Driven Workflow for Automated Process Control Strategy Generation and Tuning from Dynamic Process Models

title: Cycle-Consistent and Uncertainty-Aware Neural Surrogates for Tokamak Edge Plasmas
authors: Abdourahmane Diaw, Sebastian De Pascuale, Jae-Sun Park, Ivan Paradela Perez, Jeremy D. Lore, Stefan Dasbach
abstract: The boundary and divertor plasma govern how a tokamak exhausts power and particles, setting heat fluxes, target conditions, and the onset of detachment. Predicting these quantities is essential for operating current and future devices, but edge simulations that resolve them are too slow for parameter scans, optimization, or real-time control. Machine-learning surrogates offer a fast alternative, yet most are forward-only: they cannot recover input parameters from observations or assess the reliability of their predictions. We introduce a cycle-consistent neural surrogate for edge plasmas, combining a conditional U-Net forward model with an optimization-based inverse method built on the frozen forward network. The forward model maps five control parameters to two-dimensional plasma-state fields on the SOLPS-ITER mesh; the inverse method enforces consistency between forward and inverse predictions, a self-supervised quality check needing no ground-truth labels at inference. An ensemble of multilayer perceptrons also predicts electron temperature and density profiles at the outboard midplane and divertor targets, with uncertainty estimates that flag where more simulations are needed. The forward model achieves normalized root-mean-square errors below 2.6% and Pearson correlations above 0.95 for all fields. Cycle-consistency regularization raises the average cyclical $R^2$ from 0.59 to 0.99 without degrading forward accuracy and enables recovery of the core fueling rate; all five control parameters are recovered with Pearson $r\ge0.97$. A $k$-d tree warm start yields a database completion rate above 95%, versus roughly 30% outright failures when cold-started. With about $4\times10^6$ parameters, the model produces full 2D predictions in milliseconds, five to six orders of magnitude faster than SOLPS-ITER, enabling real-time control, parameter scans, uncertainty analysis, and digital twins.

infographic.key_insight: A cycle-consistent neural surrogate can predict tokamak edge plasma fields quickly while also recovering the underlying control inputs and estimating prediction uncertainty.
infographic.engineering_relevance: This enables near real-time edge-plasma analysis for parameter scans, optimization, control, and digital-twin workflows where full SOLPS-ITER simulations are too slow.
method: Conditional U-Net maps five control parameters to 2D SOLPS-ITER plasma-state fields.
A frozen forward model is paired with an optimization-based inverse method to enforce cycle consistency.
An ensemble MLP predicts midplane and divertor profiles with uncertainty estimates to flag missing-data regions.
infographic.evidence_signal: The forward model reports normalized RMSE below 2.6% and Pearson correlations above 0.95, while cycle-consistency raises average cyclical R² from 0.59 to 0.99 and recovers all five control parameters with Pearson r≥0.97.
infographic.watch_item: Performance may depend on database coverage and warm starts, since cold-start inverse runs had about 30% outright failures.
infographic.paper_title: Cycle-Consistent and Uncertainty-Aware Neural Surrogates for Tokamak Edge Plasmas

title: GS-Agent: Creating 4D Physical Worlds With Generative Simulation
authors: Hongxin Zhang, Chunru Lin, Junyan Li, Zhou Xian, Tsun-Hsuan Wang, Chuang Gan
abstract: Creating dynamic and physically realistic 4D worlds from natural language descriptions is both fascinating and challenging. Traditional computer graphics methods rely on manual creation, requiring extensive human effort to fine-tune materials, motions, and visual fidelity. Recent advances in generative foundation models have sparked interest in learning to generate such 4D worlds from large-scale data; however, existing methods still struggle to ensure physical plausibility and controllability. In this work, we take a different path by leveraging foundation models to construct an agentic system that emulates how humans traditionally create 4D worlds, yet automates the entire process. We present GS-Agent, an end-to-end multi-agent framework that integrates physics engines in the loop to generate realistic, dynamic, and controllable 4D physical worlds from natural language. Inspired by how humans build 4D worlds, GS-Agent decomposes the task into entity management, covering 3D asset curation, material tuning, placement, and motion control, and rendering configuration, including camera and lighting manipulation. Multiple agents with distinct expertise interact with the physics engine via code, seek multimodal feedback, and collaborate to iteratively construct 4D worlds that align with the given descriptions. Experimental results show that GS-Agent effectively converts natural language into diverse and physically plausible 4D worlds exhibiting rich interactions among liquids, deformable objects, and rigid bodies, while achieving cinematic camera and lighting control. We envision GS-Agent as a foundation for a new paradigm in 4D world generation, empowering creative content creation and physical AI. Project page at https://umass-embodied-agi.github.io/gs-agent/

infographic.key_insight: GS-Agent uses a multi-agent, physics-in-the-loop workflow to turn text prompts into physically plausible, controllable 4D worlds with dynamic interactions.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The framework automates a traditionally manual 4D content pipeline, making it relevant for generative simulation, digital twins, robotics training, and creative production.
method: Decomposes world generation into entity management and rendering configuration.
Uses multiple specialized agents to handle asset curation, material tuning, placement, motion, camera, and lighting.
Iteratively edits scenes through code and multimodal feedback from the physics engine.
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract reports that experiments produce diverse 4D worlds with realistic interactions among liquids, deformable objects, and rigid bodies, plus cinematic camera and lighting control.
infographic.watch_item: The approach depends on coordinated agents and physics-engine feedback, so robustness, runtime cost, and generalization to unseen scene types may be challenging.
infographic.paper_title: GS-Agent: Creating 4D Physical Worlds With Generative Simulation

title: Graph Learning on Ensembles of Cyclic Peptides: An Investigation of Molecular Ensemble Modeling
authors: Aaron Feller, Kris Deibler, Maxim Secor
abstract: Molecular property prediction from structure often uses a single representative conformation, even though many molecules exist as conformational ensembles in solution. We introduce EnsembleEGNN, a molecular ensemble foundation model that encodes an ensemble by first encoding each conformer with shared Equivariant Graph Neural Network (EGNN) layers, then pooling the resulting conformer representations with a Set Attention Block. We pretrain the model on CREMP, a cyclic peptide ensemble dataset, using a multi-task self-supervised objective combining masked token recovery, noisy-coordinate reconstruction, and pairwise distance reconstruction. On the CREMP-CycPeptMPDB dataset, training EnsembleEGNN from scratch fails entirely ($R^2=0.005$). However, the pretrained model reaches $R^2=0.477$ and Pearson $r=0.699$, outperforming the sequence-only BERT baseline ($R^2=0.439$, Pearson $r=0.667$). When EnsembleEGNN is co-trained end-to-end with the BERT sequence encoder, the hybrid model improves further to $R^2=0.538$ and Pearson $r=0.737$. These results demonstrate that encoding conformational ensembles into a single thermodynamically informed embedding improves cyclic-peptide property prediction.

infographic.key_insight: Modeling a molecule as a conformational ensemble, rather than a single structure, substantially improves cyclic-peptide property prediction.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The study suggests that thermodynamically informed graph embeddings can boost molecular screening and design workflows for flexible biomolecules.
method: Encode each conformer with shared EGNN layers
Pool conformer embeddings with a Set Attention Block
Pretrain with masked-token recovery, noisy-coordinate reconstruction, and pairwise distance reconstruction
infographic.evidence_signal: On CREMP-CycPeptMPDB, the pretrained EnsembleEGNN achieved R^2=0.477 and Pearson r=0.699, outperforming a sequence-only BERT baseline (R^2=0.439, r=0.667), while training from scratch failed (R^2=0.005).
infographic.watch_item: Results are shown on cyclic peptides and may not transfer directly to other molecular families without careful validation of ensemble quality and computational cost.
infographic.paper_title: Graph Learning on Ensembles of Cyclic Peptides: An Investigation of Molecular Ensemble Modeling

title: Agentic coding without the cloud: evaluating open-weight large language models on longitudinal data preparation tasks
authors: Mack Nixon, Liam Wright, Yevgeniya Kovalchuk, Alison Fang-Wei Wu, Martin Danka, Andy Boyd
abstract: Large language models (LLMs) and agents are now widely used tools in code development, with data typically sent to third-party cloud-based models. Their adoption in research using personal data is constrained by governance requirements that typically prohibit data transmission to external services. Locally deployable open-weight models offer an alternative since sensitive data never leave the local environment. We introduce an open-source framework for evaluating the efficacy of AI agents powered by open-weight LLMs on one of the most persistent bottlenecks in research on longitudinal population studies: data preparation. The framework comprises: a curated ground-truth dataset (cleaning scripts preparing six sweeps of data from a British cohort study), task definitions encompassing tasks such as category harmonization and multi-wave merging, and automated routines for evaluating the LLM-produced R code and outputted data. We benchmark LLMs across the (consumer grade) deployment spectrum to assess their efficacy in 20 data preparation tasks (creation of 102 variables). Current state-of-the-art, 31-35B parameter models almost saturated our benchmark ("average task completion" up to 87.9%). The performance of open-weight LLMs running on consumer-grade hardware shows promise of a viable path toward AI-assisted data preparation in governance-restricted research settings. Our framework is publicly available at: https://github.com/UCL-ARC/RRBench.

infographic.key_insight: Open-weight, locally run LLM agents can nearly automate complex longitudinal data-preparation workflows without sending sensitive research data to the cloud.
infographic.engineering_relevance: This suggests a practical pathway for governance-restricted studies to use AI-assisted code generation and data cleaning on consumer-grade hardware.
method: Built an open-source benchmark from ground-truth R scripts for six sweeps of a British cohort study.
Defined 20 data-preparation tasks, including category harmonization and multi-wave merging, spanning 102 variables.
Evaluated LLM-generated R code and resulting outputs with automated scoring routines.
infographic.evidence_signal: In the benchmark, state-of-the-art 31–35B open-weight models nearly saturated performance, reaching up to 87.9% average task completion.
infographic.watch_item: Strong benchmark results may not fully translate to messy real-world datasets, where edge cases, domain rules, and verification overhead can still limit safe deployment.
infographic.paper_title: Agentic coding without the cloud: evaluating open-weight large language models on longitudinal data preparation tasks

title: Semantic-Aware Task Clustering for Constructive and Cooperative Multi-Tasking
authors: Ahmad Halimi Razlighi, Maximilian H. V. Tillmann, Edgar Beck, Bho Matthiesen, Armin Dekorsy
abstract: Cooperative multi-task semantic communication (CMT-SemCom) improves task execution performance by leveraging shared representations. However, as we demonstrated in [1], cooperative multi-tasking can be either constructive or destructive, depending on the semantic relationships among tasks. To ensure constructive cooperation, we propose a semantic-aware task clustering method for CMT-SemCom. We have formulated a sequential multi-stage optimization problem in which semantically aligned tasks are clustered once after a short initial training phase, and then end-to-end (E2E) joint training is conducted exclusively within the discovered groups. Specifically, the problem decomposes into two stages: (i) a semantic clustering problem leveraging hierarchical density-based spatial clustering, and (ii) an intra-cluster E2E CMT-SemCom learning problem. Simulation results demonstrate that the proposed framework effectively mitigates destructive cooperation and negative transfer, yielding accuracy gains compared to unclustered multi-tasking and individual training baselines.

infographic.key_insight: Semantic-aware clustering can separate tasks that help each other from tasks that interfere, enabling constructive cooperative multi-task semantic communication.
infographic.engineering_relevance: For scientific machine learning systems, this provides a practical way to reduce negative transfer and improve multi-task performance by grouping semantically aligned tasks before joint end-to-end training.
method: Short initial training to extract task representations.
Hierarchical density-based clustering to discover semantically aligned task groups.
End-to-end multi-task semantic communication training performed only within each cluster.
infographic.evidence_signal: Simulation results in the abstract report accuracy gains over both unclustered multi-tasking and individual-training baselines.
infographic.watch_item: The approach depends on a reliable early semantic representation and a clustering step whose quality may affect downstream grouping and performance.
infographic.paper_title: Semantic-Aware Task Clustering for Constructive and Cooperative Multi-Tasking

title: ElasticTTT: Prior-Preserving Test-Time Tuning for Video Editing
authors: Yueyi Liu, Chi Zhang, Sen Cui, Miao Liu
abstract: Test-Time Tuning (TTT) on pretrained diffusion models has emerged as a powerful paradigm for video editing. However, there exists a foundational mismatch between the distribution-mapping nature of generative models and the single-point optimization of standard TTT. In this paper, we demonstrate that this mismatch triggers \textit{Prior Collapse}, a degenerate state where the model discards the text conditions and spatial latents, collapsing generations to the source video, or entangling the features of distinct regions. To resolve this, we propose \textbf{ElasticTTT}, a novel framework that preserves the prior generative distribution and rescues generative elasticity. Specifically, we propose \textit{Target Distribution Regularization} to prevent sharp memorization minima, \textit{Contrastive CFG} to guide inference away from source biases, and \textit{Asynchronous Noise Schedule} to preserve unedited regions. Extensive evaluations, supported by theoretical analysis, demonstrate that ElasticTTT successfully preserves the generative prior of the base model, achieving state-of-the-art performance on one-shot video editing.

infographic.key_insight: ElasticTTT fixes test-time tuning for video editing by preserving the pretrained diffusion prior, preventing collapse back to the source video or feature entanglement.
infographic.engineering_relevance: This provides a practical way to adapt pretrained video diffusion models at inference time while maintaining editability, spatial consistency, and stronger one-shot editing results.
method: Target Distribution Regularization: avoids sharp memorization minima during tuning.
Contrastive CFG: steers generation away from source-video biases.
Asynchronous Noise Schedule: protects unedited regions during editing.
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract reports extensive evaluations and theoretical analysis showing state-of-the-art performance on one-shot video editing while preserving the base model prior.
infographic.watch_item: The method adds inference-time tuning complexity, so stability and hyperparameter sensitivity may be important in real deployments.
infographic.paper_title: ElasticTTT: Prior-Preserving Test-Time Tuning for Video Editing

title: Euclid-MCP: A Model Context Protocol Server for Deterministic Logical Reasoning via Prolog
authors: Bartolomeo Bogliolo
abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) excel at natural language understanding and generation but remain unreliable for multi-step logical reasoning, especially in safety-critical or compliance-sensitive domains. Recent neuro-symbolic approaches address this gap by coupling neural models with external symbolic engines, yet most integrations are bespoke and lack a standardized interface for tool-augmented agents. This paper presents Euclid-MCP, an open-source MCP server that provides deterministic logical reasoning via SWI-Prolog. Euclid-MCP introduces Euclid-IR, an engine-agnostic intermediate representation for Horn-clause logic that is human-readable, easy for LLMs to generate, and straightforward to compile into Prolog or alternative backends. The server exposes a compact tool interface that supports a translate-run-inspect-repair loop, enabling LLM clients to delegate inference while retaining full access to proof traces and derivation logs. We evaluate Euclid-MCP on a realistic IT security and compliance use case. Results show that while LLMs alone are sufficient on small knowledge bases, they hallucinate systematically on larger problems, whereas Euclid-MCP delivers exact answers with lower latency and more compact outputs. We argue that semantic RAG is fundamentally unsuited for rule enforcement, and that Euclid-MCP can serve as a stable, shared reasoning substrate for both RAG-based assistants and agentic systems.

infographic.key_insight: Euclid-MCP wraps deterministic Prolog reasoning in a standardized MCP tool server, letting LLMs offload multi-step logic while preserving proof traces and repair loops.
infographic.engineering_relevance: It offers a reusable, engine-agnostic way to add exact rule-based inference to agents and RAG systems in compliance- and safety-sensitive workflows.
method: Defines Euclid-IR, a human-readable Horn-clause intermediate representation.
Compiles Euclid-IR to SWI-Prolog or other backends for deterministic inference.
Exposes a translate-run-inspect-repair tool loop with proof and derivation logs.
infographic.evidence_signal: The paper reports evaluation on an IT security/compliance use case, finding that LLMs work on small knowledge bases but hallucinate on larger ones, while Euclid-MCP returns exact answers with lower latency and more compact outputs.
infographic.watch_item: Adoption depends on correct rule encoding and backend compilation, so errors in Euclid-IR translation or Prolog knowledge maintenance could still undermine results.
infographic.paper_title: Euclid-MCP: A Model Context Protocol Server for Deterministic Logical Reasoning via Prolog

title: Benchmarking Agents for Proving Theorems in Quantum Algorithms and Quantum Information
authors: Lei Zhang, Yusheng Zhao, Yimeng Cao, Ranyiliu Chen, Mingrui Jing, Jizhe Lai
abstract: Formal verification is becoming increasingly practical for quantum computing, yet the ability of AI agents to construct machine-checkable proofs in this domain remains unmeasured. We introduce Lean-QuantumAlg-Bench and Lean-QIT-Bench, two Lean 4 benchmarks containing 36 and 40 theorem-completion tasks for quantum algorithms and quantum information theory, respectively. Every task compiles in a fixed environment and is evaluated by deterministic proof checking and targeted semantic review, with difficulty weights assigned before model execution. We evaluate four models-GPT-5.5, Kimi K3, DeepSeek V4-Pro, and MiniMax M3-within a common theorem-proving framework under two settings: a task-only baseline and library-augmented deduction (LAD), which additionally provides access to a verified domain library. The highest difficulty-weighted scores are 60.4 out of 100 on the quantum-algorithm benchmark and 59.6 out of 100 on the quantum-information benchmark. LAD improves both score and completion rate in all eight model-benchmark comparisons, with gains of up to 15.9 points, providing evidence that verified libraries can strengthen domain-specific proof agents. The results reveal recurring weaknesses of agentic proving in areas such as quantum simulation, quantum learning, quantum information measures, and entanglement theory. Monetary and wall-clock costs per score point also vary substantially across models, highlighting important capability-efficiency trade-offs. We expect these benchmarks to establish a reproducible baseline for developing more capable and reliable proof agents, and to pave the way toward self-evolving AI scientists for advancing quantum information science.

infographic.key_insight: The paper introduces two Lean 4 benchmarks to measure how well AI agents can generate machine-checkable proofs in quantum algorithms and quantum information, showing that verified libraries significantly improve performance.
infographic.engineering_relevance: These benchmarks provide a reproducible testbed for building more reliable theorem-proving agents for quantum science, where formal correctness matters for future quantum software and research automation.
method: Created Lean-QuantumAlg-Bench (36 tasks) and Lean-QIT-Bench (40 tasks) covering theorem completion in quantum algorithms and quantum information.
Evaluated four models under two settings: task-only baseline and library-augmented deduction (LAD) with access to a verified domain library.
Used deterministic proof checking plus targeted semantic review, with difficulty weights assigned before model execution.
infographic.evidence_signal: Across eight model-benchmark comparisons, LAD improved both score and completion rate, with top difficulty-weighted scores of 60.4/100 and 59.6/100 on the two benchmarks.
infographic.watch_item: Results depend on a fixed Lean environment and benchmark-specific task distribution, so generalization to broader quantum theorem proving or different formal systems may be limited.
infographic.paper_title: Benchmarking Agents for Proving Theorems in Quantum Algorithms and Quantum Information

title: AI Assistants Overassist
authors: Verona Teo, Raghav Jain, Tobias Gerstenberg, Max Kleiman-Weiner
abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used as tutors and thought partners, helping users reason through problems. While guidance from AI assistants can scaffold thinking and foster learning, such benefits depend on how they help--for instance, intervening too early or too frequently may hinder true learning and cognitive engagement. Yet how AI systems navigate intervention decisions during problem-solving remains poorly understood. Here, we introduce Int-Bench, a simulation-based benchmark for evaluating LLM interventions during learning. Int-Bench simulates a "student" solving a problem while a "teacher" monitors the student's reasoning and decides whether, when, and how to intervene. Across three domains--code debugging, mathematics, and brain teasers--we evaluate LLM teachers on the frequency and timing of interventions, as well as their impact on both immediate task success and generalization to new problems. We also compare LLMs to humans, finding that LLMs intervene more frequently and earlier than humans. Moreover, in contrast to humans, they tend to provide complete solutions rather than targeted hints. These findings suggest that current LLM assistants often optimize for short-term success rather than supporting the reasoning processes needed for deeper learning and long-term success.

infographic.key_insight: LLM tutors often over-intervene—acting too early and too frequently—so they may boost immediate success at the expense of deeper learning.
infographic.engineering_relevance: For AI assistant design, this suggests intervention policies should optimize for timely, minimal hints rather than full solutions to support human reasoning and generalization.
method: Built Int-Bench, a simulation benchmark with a "student" and a monitoring "teacher".
Evaluated LLM intervention choices across code debugging, mathematics, and brain teasers.
Compared intervention frequency, timing, and downstream effects against human behavior.
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract reports cross-domain evaluation of LLM teachers on intervention rate/timing plus immediate task success and generalization to new problems.
infographic.watch_item: Simulation-based results may not fully capture real learner needs or classroom dynamics, so human-centered validation is still needed.
infographic.paper_title: AI Assistants Overassist

title: Expert Behavior Prior Reinforcement Learning
authors: Gong Gao, Weidong Zhao, Xianhui Liu, Ning Jia
abstract: Behavior prior reinforcement learning (BPRL) has emerged as a promising paradigm to improve sample efficiency in online reinforcement learning (RL) by leveraging policy priors derived from offline demonstrations. However, most existing BPRL methods rely on static offline datasets, which often suffer from low data diversity and suboptimal trajectory quality. This reliance restricts the effectiveness of policy priors, hindering both policy exploitation and stability during online training. Consequently, agents are prone to inefficient exploration and unstable learning dynamics. To address these limitations, we deviate from existing offline pre-training methods and propose an Expert Behavior Prior (EBP) algorithm. Specifically, we introduce a Q-guided conditional variational autoencoder (Q-CVAE) that learns to generate expert policy priors directly from the online replay buffer. This enables the generation of high-value actions for guiding policy updates without relying on pre-collected expert trajectories. To further enhance policy exploitation, we propose an expert policy guidance (EPG) mechanism that selects expert actions from a generative support set, and we integrate a policy gradient correction (PGC) module to harmonize Q-guidance with expert supervision, promoting stable and consistent policy improvement. Extensive experiments conducted on robotic control (Gym, PyBullet) and industrial control (DMControl) benchmarks demonstrate that EBP significantly outperforms state-of-the-art online RL algorithms, achieving higher sample efficiency and more stable convergence.

infographic.key_insight: Expert Behavior Prior RL learns expert-like action priors from the online replay buffer, improving exploration, stability, and sample efficiency without needing offline expert trajectories.
infographic.engineering_relevance: This is relevant for autonomous robotics and industrial control because it offers a more practical way to stabilize online RL when high-quality demonstration data is limited or unavailable.
method: Q-CVAE generates high-value expert policy priors from the online replay buffer.
Expert Policy Guidance (EPG) selects actions from a generative support set to strengthen policy exploitation.
Policy Gradient Correction (PGC) aligns Q-guidance with expert supervision for stable updates.
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract reports extensive benchmarks on Gym, PyBullet, and DMControl, where EBP outperforms state-of-the-art online RL methods with better sample efficiency and more stable convergence.
infographic.watch_item: Performance may depend on accurate Q-guidance and well-tuned generative support, so instability or bias in value estimates could affect action prior quality.
infographic.paper_title: Expert Behavior Prior Reinforcement Learning

title: Expanding Flow Maps
authors: Sophia Tang, Pranam Chatterjee
abstract: Flow-based generative models have enabled remarkable progress in fast and controllable generation across continuous and discrete state spaces, yet existing parameterizations are constrained to fixed dimensions or fixed sequence lengths. Here, we introduce Expanding Generative Flows (EFlows), which define flows between distributions of increasing dimensionality along an expanding interpolant that grows the state by augmenting it with conditional noise. Building on this construction, we propose Expanding Flow Maps (EFMs), a new class of flow maps that distill the expanding interpolant into efficient few-step generative models. Each EFM factors the map between any two timesteps into two learnable operations: an expand operator, which augments the state space with new coordinates or tokens conditioned on the current state, and a transport map, which pushes the expanded state forward along the interpolant. Composing these operators yields a single map that jointly expands and denoises the state, recovering existing fixed-canvas flows and flow maps as the special case in which the expand operator is the identity. We further extend the framework to the discrete simplex, enabling variable-size graph generation and variable-length sequence generation. Across both continuous and discrete modalities, we establish EFlows and EFMs as a principled framework for settings in which output size is itself a learned, controllable degree of freedom.

infographic.key_insight: Expanding Generative Flows and Expanding Flow Maps learn to generate outputs whose size can grow during the generation process, rather than assuming a fixed canvas or fixed sequence length.
infographic.engineering_relevance: This enables controllable variable-size generation for both continuous and discrete problems, including images, graphs, and sequences, with a unified flow-based framework.
method: Introduce an expanding interpolant that adds conditional noise to increase dimensionality over time.
Factor each map into an expand operator plus a transport map to jointly add dimensions and denoise.
Extend the construction to the discrete simplex for variable-size graph and sequence generation.
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract reports broad applicability across continuous and discrete modalities, with special cases recovering existing fixed-size flows and flow maps.
infographic.watch_item: Practical performance may depend on how well the expand operator is trained to add meaningful new coordinates or tokens without destabilizing the transport step.
infographic.paper_title: Expanding Flow Maps

title: Agent-Guided Relational Concept Discovery: Toward Interpretable Surgical Margin Assessment
authors: Nooshin Maghsoodi, Amoon Jamzad, Robert Policelli, Mohammad Farahmand, Dilakshan Srikanthan, Martin Kaufmann
abstract: Deep learning models can effectively use Rapid Evaporative Ionization Mass Spectrometry (REIMS) data for surgical margin assessment. However, their clinical adoption remains challenging due to limited generalization to operating room conditions. This difficulty arises because models are typically trained on labeled spectra collected from resected tissue samples, while they must operate on noisy, unlabeled data acquired directly during surgery. In addition, the black-box nature of deep learning models makes it difficult to understand and systematically improve their behavior. Concept-based learning offers a promising way to address these challenges by mapping raw measurements to human-understandable concepts. However, supervised concept-based approaches rely on concept annotations, which are difficult to obtain in complex mass spectrometry workflows. We propose Agent-Guided Concept Discovery, a framework that learns meaningful concepts directly from data without requiring predefined concept labels. During training, a reasoning agent refines semantic descriptions of the learned concepts and adaptively adjusts their weight based on diagnostic relevance. These concepts are further grounded using a biochemical knowledge graph to ensure consistency with known metabolic relationships. Across Skin and Breast Cancer datasets, our model improves balanced accuracy and sensitivity over the baseline. In a representative intraoperative case, it shows fewer false positives, indicating better generalization to surgical conditions.

infographic.key_insight: The paper introduces Agent-Guided Relational Concept Discovery, which learns interpretable concepts directly from REIMS data to improve surgical margin assessment without requiring concept labels.
infographic.engineering_relevance: It targets a key deployment gap in surgical AI by making models more robust to intraoperative noise while adding concept-level interpretability for clinical trust and debugging.
method: Learn concepts from unlabeled mass spectrometry spectra instead of relying on predefined annotations.
Use a reasoning agent to refine semantic descriptions of concepts and adjust their diagnostic importance during training.
Ground discovered concepts with a biochemical knowledge graph to align them with known metabolic relationships.
infographic.evidence_signal: Across Skin and Breast Cancer datasets, the model improves balanced accuracy and sensitivity over the baseline, and a representative intraoperative case shows fewer false positives.
infographic.watch_item: Concept grounding and agent-guided refinement may add system complexity and still require careful validation to ensure learned concepts remain clinically meaningful across sites and devices.
infographic.paper_title: Agent-Guided Relational Concept Discovery: Toward Interpretable Surgical Margin Assessment

title: Bridging the Gap Between Plausibility and Admissibility: Constraint-Aware Flow Maps for Dynamic Graph Systems
authors: Michael Romei de Socio, Gian Luca Pozzato, Alessio Merlo
abstract: Generative models can support decision-making under uncertainty by producing ensembles of plausible future system trajectories, but statistical plausibility does not ensure structural feasibility. This study investigates whether post-sampling symbolic constraints can improve the reliability of generative trajectory modeling in dynamic graph-structured systems. A conditional diffusion model generates future graph-state trajectories from partial observations, while an external symbolic layer applies hard filtering, soft weighting, or projection-based repair. The framework is evaluated on two controlled synthetic regimes: a compact graph and a medium-complexity dependency graph, using metrics for structural validity, sample efficiency, diversity, robustness, and calibration. In the compact regime, the model produces an invalid probability mass of 0.002996, indicating an almost entirely admissible trajectory manifold. Under the same architecture and training protocol, invalid mass increases to 0.155929 in the medium-complexity regime. Hard filtering removes all invalid retained trajectories while preserving 84.4% of generated samples, whereas soft weighting preserves effective sample size but yields only limited validity gains. Family-level analysis shows that dependency constraints account for nearly all observed inadmissibility. These results indicate that statistical plausibility and structural admissibility are distinct reliability properties and that symbolic constraint handling becomes more valuable as graph-structural complexity increases.

infographic.key_insight: Post-sampling symbolic constraints turn a plausible diffusion-based trajectory generator into a more admissible one, especially when graph structure becomes complex.
infographic.engineering_relevance: For dynamic graph systems in decision support, combining generative models with constraint handling can improve reliability without discarding the benefits of sampling-based uncertainty modeling.
method: Conditional diffusion model generates future graph-state trajectories from partial observations.
External symbolic layer enforces constraints via hard filtering, soft weighting, or projection-based repair.
Evaluation compares structural validity, sample efficiency, diversity, robustness, and calibration on two synthetic graph regimes.
infographic.evidence_signal: Invalid probability mass rises from 0.002996 in the compact graph to 0.155929 in the medium-complexity graph; hard filtering removes all invalid retained trajectories while preserving 84.4% of generated samples.
infographic.watch_item: Constraint repair or filtering may reduce invalidity, but it can also affect diversity and effective sample size, so deployment should balance admissibility against sampling efficiency.
infographic.paper_title: Bridging the Gap Between Plausibility and Admissibility: Constraint-Aware Flow Maps for Dynamic Graph Systems

title: Same Dangerous Objective, Opposite Advice: Direct Exposure versus Multi-Agent Mediation
authors: Linjun Li
abstract: Even a current high-capability LLM can appear safer when shown a dangerous objective directly than when other agents transform and relay its direction. Using OpenAI's gpt-5.6-sol model alias, we test 25 pre-specified mirrored trade-off profiles. Direct exposure to an objective authorizing concealment, fabrication, and pressure produced advice net opposed to its target. After an Id and Censor transformed the same objective into affect and a constraint-rewritten, target-bearing intention, the user-facing Superego---which saw the preferred direction but not the raw objective, its manipulative clauses, or its source---produced advice net aligned with the target. This behavioral reverse shift is consistent with the model recognizing or distrusting the manipulative motive, although we do not identify its internal mechanism. The second result exposes a compositional safety gap: a current high-capability model can be used as the user-facing component of an automated, multi-stage workflow serving an explicitly manipulative objective. The workflow can keep the raw instruction, its manipulation-authorizing clauses, and its provenance outside the downstream model's context while preserving the objective's target direction. A user with endpoint-only access likewise cannot directly inspect those upstream messages including the objective.

infographic.key_insight: A high-capability LLM can reject a dangerous objective when exposed to it directly, yet align with the same objective when it is transformed and relayed through intermediary agents.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Multi-agent pipelines can hide manipulative intent upstream while still producing user-facing outputs that follow the target direction, creating a compositional safety gap for deployed AI systems.
method: Tested 25 pre-specified mirrored trade-off profiles with OpenAI's gpt-5.6-sol alias.
Compared direct exposure to a dangerous objective versus a mediated workflow using Id, Censor, and a user-facing Superego.
Evaluated whether advice was net opposed to or aligned with the target direction.
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract reports that direct exposure produced advice net opposed to the target, while the mediated setup produced advice net aligned with the target across 25 mirrored profiles.
infographic.watch_item: The study shows behavioral reversal but does not identify the model's internal mechanism, so results may depend on the specific model, prompting, and workflow design.
infographic.paper_title: Same Dangerous Objective, Opposite Advice: Direct Exposure versus Multi-Agent Mediation
